masthead.kicker: Hidden Champions of India / a DeepThought series

headline.text: Dr. Sabharwal's Wound Care: a four-decade family manufacturer, formally incorporated for the first time.

subhead.text: A Baddi, Himachal Pradesh manufacturer of surgical dressings and transdermal patches, holding an active, independently-confirmed ISO 13485 medical-device certification.

p1_engine.eyebrow: A confirmed capability, ahead of a track record

blocks.text: Dr Sabharwal's Wound Care Private Limited was incorporated on 13 March 2024 — but this is a formal-entity conversion, not a startup. The underlying business has run under the Sabharwal family's wound-care brand since 1984, most recently as a proprietorship under Manish Sabharwal, who now sits on the new company's board alongside Ajit Rai Sabharwal and one other director.

As a newly formed entity its filed financial history is thin: revenue for the year ending March 2025 falls in the under-₹10-crore bracket, on ₹15 lakh authorized and ₹1 lakh paid-up capital — too early to read a growth trend from, and not comparable to the decades-old family brand behind it.

What **is** confirmed, independently: an active ISO 13485:2016 medical-device quality-management certificate (No. IN55405H), verified directly on IAF CertSearch, whose registered scope — design, development, manufacture and marketing of medicated and non-medicated, sterile and non-sterile surgical dressings, plasters, bandages, and transdermal drug-delivery patches — matches the company's actual product line exactly.

The company also lists ISO 9001 and GMP certification on its own site and describes itself as US FDA audited, exporting to 40–50 countries. These are the company's own claims, not yet independently registry-checked the way the ISO 13485 certificate was — and no CDSCO (India's medical-device regulator) registration could be confirmed for this facility.

p2_market.eyebrow: A large field, in its slower-growing tier

insights.point: The wound-care field it sells into is **large, and counted differently by different houses.**
insights.evidence: Estimates for 2026 range from ~$23.9B to ~$26.1B globally, growing at anywhere from 4.3% to 7.5% a year depending on scope and source.
insights.source: Coherent Market Insights; Fortune Business Insights; Grand View Research; MarketsandMarkets

insights.point: But the company's own product line sits in the **slower, more traditional tier.**
insights.evidence: Advanced wound dressings — foam, antimicrobial, alginate — hold an estimated 44.27% share of the market in 2026 and are growing fastest. This company's gauze, tape, cotton, bandages and plasters sit in the older, more commoditized traditional tier.

insights.point: Both hospital and distributor buyers gate on the same thing: **certification, not just price.**
insights.evidence: ISO 13485, CE marking, and US FDA compliance are named as what make Indian manufacturers 'preferred partners for global procurement' in this category — exactly the certificate this company can now independently prove is active.

reflect.text: A small, family-run, newly-formalized manufacturer with one genuinely confirmed asset — an active, scope-matched medical-device certification — competing in the traditional, slower-growing tier of a market whose fastest growth is happening one tier up.

p2_market.sourceNote: Market data: Coherent Market Insights, Fortune Business Insights, Grand View Research, MarketsandMarkets, Technavio. Estimates vary widely by scope; ranges shown.

p3_opportunities.lede: Three places worth a closer look, each built on the one thing already confirmed: a real, active, scope-matched certification.

items.title: Move up into advanced dressings
items.body: The certified quality system that supports sterile, medicated dressings is largely the same infrastructure advanced dressings need. That tier is growing faster than the traditional gauze-and-bandage line this company currently sells.
items.source: Certification scope: IAF CertSearch. Market-tier growth: wound-care market research aggregators.

items.title: Build the new entity's own track record
items.body: Financial history now resets with a 2-year-old legal entity. A clean, promptly-filed set of accounts builds the credit history a decades-old proprietorship never needed but a scaling exporter does — for working capital and export-finance lines.

items.title: Confirm and formalize CDSCO registration
items.body: No CDSCO (India's medical-device regulator) registration could be confirmed for this facility. Settling this — either finding it already exists or filing for it — is what would open India's own domestic hospital/institutional channel alongside the export business.
items.source: CDSCO MD Online search — no confirmation found either way.

guesslabel.text: Possibilities, not prescriptions. Which would work, and how much, only the company's own data and people can tell. Each is small, made to learn fast.

items.title: Pilot one advanced-dressing SKU
items.body: Use the existing certified quality system to trial a single foam or antimicrobial dressing product, and test buyer interest before committing to the full line.

items.title: File a clean first set of annual accounts
items.body: Get the new Pvt Ltd's first full financial year filed cleanly and promptly — the track record that unlocks working-capital and export-finance lines a proprietorship couldn't access the same way.

items.title: Confirm CDSCO status directly
items.body: A same-week regulatory check — not resolvable from public search — on whether the Baddi facility already holds a CDSCO manufacturing license, or needs to file for one, before leaning into India's domestic institutional channel.

takeaway.text: One fact here is not a claim — it's a registry entry: an active, scope-matched medical-device certification, on a manufacturer whose corporate track record is only just beginning. **The capability is decades old. The company, on paper, is two years old.** What it does with that gap is the story worth watching.
